records.summary: This first case establishes the baseline mental model that later sources can refine rather than creating disconnected summaries.

items.label: Controlled execution
items.source_basis: The talk argues that production agent work needs authority, durable history, protected data access, intervention and replay around model execution.
items.prior_basis: No earlier Signal to Insight evidence existed; this is the baseline case.
items.interpretation: The source creates the project's initial controlled-execution model rather than merely adding another agent implementation detail.

items.label: Execution history
items.source_basis: A durable record of consequential work is presented as necessary for reconstruction, governance and later evaluation.
items.prior_basis: No earlier project concept covered reconstructable execution history.
items.interpretation: Execution history becomes a reusable concept that later workflow and policy sources can make more concrete.

records.summary: Temporal turns the earlier generic idea of durable, reconstructable execution into a concrete workflow-runtime model.

items.label: Durable execution
items.source_basis: Temporal persists Workflow Execution progress as Event History while replaceable Workers execute tasks from Task Queues.
items.prior_basis: The enterprise-agent case introduced durable execution as a desirable production property but did not explain a concrete runtime mechanism.
items.interpretation: Temporal narrows the abstract property into a specific mechanism: state survives outside any one Worker process and can be reconstructed from history.

items.label: Execution history
items.source_basis: Temporal defines Event History as an append-only record representing Workflow Execution state and progress.
items.prior_basis: Execution history was already present as a general governance and replay concept.
items.interpretation: The source makes the concept operational by showing one system where history is also the mechanism for workflow-state reconstruction.

items.label: Idempotency under retry
items.source_basis: Activity work can be retried, so external effects still need safe or idempotent semantics.
items.prior_basis: The earlier agent architecture did not yet model repeated side effects under workflow retry.
items.interpretation: This adds an important boundary: durable orchestration does not make external side effects exactly-once by itself.

records.summary: OPA makes two previously broad governance ideas more precise: policy can be explicit code, and deciding permission is different from enforcing the action.

items.label: Policy as code
items.source_basis: OPA evaluates declarative Rego policy and data against structured input and returns a decision to the integrating application.
items.prior_basis: Policy as code was previously introduced only as one useful control around agent execution.
items.interpretation: OPA turns the broad idea into a concrete architecture with a policy engine, policy/data lifecycle and an explicit decision interface.

items.label: Controlled execution
items.source_basis: The application keeps ownership of the protected action while OPA computes a policy decision from explicit input, policy and data.
items.prior_basis: Controlled execution already required explicit authority around consequential work.
items.interpretation: OPA supplies a concrete authorization component compatible with that model without pretending the policy engine itself executes or verifies the business action.

items.label: Policy decision / enforcement separation
items.source_basis: OPA returns decisions; the integrating service remains responsible for enforcement and the protected operation.
items.prior_basis: The project had policy and control concepts but not this explicit architectural boundary.
items.interpretation: This becomes a reusable design test: identify who decides, who enforces and who owns the side effect.

records.summary: ReAct does not replace the production control model; it clarifies a different layer: how a model updates its next action using reasoning and external observations.

items.label: Controlled execution
items.source_basis: ReAct interleaves reasoning, environment actions and observations inside the model's task trajectory.
items.prior_basis: Controlled execution describes authorization, safe execution, reconstruction and verification around consequential work.
items.interpretation: The source refines the boundary by separating a cognitive/action-selection loop from the production substrate that governs whether and how selected actions may execute.

items.label: ReAct loop
items.source_basis: Thought, action and returned observation are interleaved so each observation can change the next reasoning/action choice.
items.prior_basis: No existing concept described this model-level feedback loop.
items.interpretation: The loop becomes a reusable mental model for agent reasoning, distinct from orchestration durability and authorization.

items.label: Observation grounding
items.source_basis: External actions return observations that provide new evidence and can correct or redirect subsequent reasoning.
items.prior_basis: Earlier project knowledge emphasized control and replay rather than environment feedback inside a reasoning trajectory.
items.interpretation: This adds the idea that tool use is valuable not only for action but also for grounding the next internal decision.

records.summary: This source opens a genuinely new learning-science branch; the agent correctly rejected attractive but irrelevant links to the existing agent/policy graph.

items.label: Retrieval practice
items.source_basis: Attempting to retrieve learned material can improve delayed retention compared with additional study, even when repeated study looks better immediately.
items.prior_basis: The existing graph contained architecture, policy and agent concepts but no learning-science model of retrieval as a learning event.
items.interpretation: This creates a new branch that changes the product itself: an explainer should later test whether the central model can be reconstructed, not only whether it was easy to read.

items.label: Immediate performance / delayed retention gap
items.source_basis: The study shows that a method can rank better on an immediate test yet worse after a meaningful delay.
items.prior_basis: No prior project concept distinguished immediate comprehension/performance from retained understanding.
items.interpretation: This becomes a product metric boundary: immediate clarity is insufficient evidence that Signal to Insight improved learning.

items.label: Metacognitive confidence gap
items.source_basis: Learners' predictions of future remembering can diverge from what they actually recall later.
items.prior_basis: The project previously had no explicit model for confidence being a weak proxy for retention.
items.interpretation: The product should measure delayed reconstruction rather than relying on a user's immediate feeling that an explainer was clear.

records.summary: Kubernetes adds a distinct state-convergence model rather than another durable-workflow mechanism: the source introduces reconciliation, desired state and observed state while the retrieved Temporal/control concepts are deliberately suppressed as different responsibilities.

items.label: Reconciliation loop
items.source_basis: The Kubernetes controller pattern repeatedly observes current state and makes or requests changes that move the system toward desired state.
items.prior_basis: The existing graph models durable workflow progress, execution control and agent loops, but it does not model persistent convergence of a declared state invariant.
items.interpretation: Reconciliation becomes a separate reusable automation model: success is not one completed run but continued correction whenever reality drifts from the target.

items.label: Desired state
items.source_basis: A Kubernetes resource specification declares what state should be true independently of what is currently true.
items.prior_basis: No prior concept explicitly represented a declarative target state as the reference point for continuous corrective automation.
items.interpretation: Separating target state from execution history makes it possible to reason about drift after any individual workflow or command has finished.

items.label: Observed state
items.source_basis: Controllers use feedback about current reality to determine whether corrective action is required before observing again.
items.prior_basis: Earlier graph concepts record execution state or observations inside other mechanisms, but not the current-state side of a desired-versus-observed convergence loop.
items.interpretation: Observed state becomes the feedback half of reconciliation and prevents declarative intent from being mistaken for proof that the system is actually correct.

records.summary: The source does not create a second idempotency concept; it refines the existing idempotency-under-retry model with a concrete receiver-side protocol based on stable logical request identity, duplicate detection and prior-outcome reuse.

items.label: Idempotency under retry
items.source_basis: Idempotent Receiver identifies repeated client requests and avoids processing the same logical operation again when a retry follows an ambiguous failure.
items.prior_basis: The Temporal case already established that retried external effects need duplicate-safe/idempotent semantics, but it did not specify a receiver protocol for recognizing the same logical mutation.
items.interpretation: The source makes the earlier boundary operational: safe retry needs a receiver-visible identity for the logical request plus durable knowledge of the prior outcome.

items.label: Idempotent Receiver
items.source_basis: The receiver checks whether the same client/request identity was already processed and returns the saved response instead of processing the mutation again.
items.prior_basis: No earlier graph concept represented a concrete receiver-side duplicate-detection and response-reuse pattern.
items.interpretation: This becomes one implementation pattern for achieving the broader idempotency-under-retry requirement at an API/service boundary.

items.label: Logical request identity
items.source_basis: The pattern identifies both the client and each request so a retry can be recognized as the same logical operation.
items.prior_basis: The existing retry model did not yet represent identity as a first-class part of duplicate-safe execution.
items.interpretation: Request identity separates repeated delivery of one intended operation from a new operation that merely looks similar.

records.summary: SQLite WAL opens a new database-storage branch: append-first commit, checkpointing and reader snapshot boundaries. All retrieved execution/audit-history matches are suppressed because shared log vocabulary does not imply the same mechanism or purpose.

items.label: Write-ahead log
items.source_basis: SQLite preserves the database file during commit and appends changed pages plus a commit record to a separate WAL.
items.prior_basis: The project graph had execution and workflow histories but no transactional database write-ahead-log concept.
items.interpretation: The log is a storage/commit mechanism that separates foreground append from later consolidation, not a business audit record.

items.label: Checkpointing
items.source_basis: SQLite later transfers committed WAL content into the database through a distinct checkpoint operation that can pause behind active readers.
items.prior_basis: No earlier concept represented WAL-to-database consolidation as a separate maintenance phase.
items.interpretation: Checkpointing makes the cost shift explicit: fast append-oriented commits still require later consolidation and coordination with readers.

items.label: WAL reader snapshot
items.source_basis: Each read transaction fixes an end mark and ignores newer WAL commits for the duration of that transaction.
items.prior_basis: Existing graph concepts did not model SQLite's point-in-time reader boundary over a concurrently growing WAL.
items.interpretation: The end mark explains why a reader can stay stable while a writer continues to append new commits.

records.summary: PostgreSQL opens a new database-concurrency branch: multiversion visibility snapshots, isolation-dependent snapshot scope and serialization retry. The existing SQLite WAL reader snapshot is explicitly rejected as the same concept because it is a WAL end-mark mechanism rather than PostgreSQL row-version visibility.

items.label: Multiversion Concurrency Control (MVCC)
items.source_basis: PostgreSQL maintains multiple data versions so statements can read a coherent snapshot while concurrent transactions continue to update data.
items.prior_basis: The graph had database storage and WAL concepts but no general multiversion concurrency model.
items.interpretation: MVCC becomes the reusable model for separating read visibility from concurrent physical updates without equating concurrency with absence of conflicts.

items.label: MVCC snapshot
items.source_basis: Each PostgreSQL statement sees a snapshot of data, and stronger isolation levels extend the stability of that view across the transaction.
items.prior_basis: SQLite WAL already had a reader end-mark concept, but it is specific to WAL visibility and is not a PostgreSQL MVCC row-version snapshot.
items.interpretation: The new snapshot concept is kept separate so similar user-visible stability does not erase the different storage and visibility mechanisms.

items.label: Transaction isolation scope
items.source_basis: Read Committed takes a snapshot at each statement, while Repeatable Read keeps a transaction snapshot and Serializable adds stronger anomaly protection.
items.prior_basis: No prior concept modeled snapshot lifetime and anomaly guarantees as an explicit isolation-level contract.
items.interpretation: Isolation scope becomes the bridge between the abstract snapshot model and application-visible consistency behavior.

items.label: Serialization failure and retry
items.source_basis: Repeatable Read and Serializable can abort transactions under concurrent conflicts, and Serializable applications must be prepared to retry transactions after serialization failure.
items.prior_basis: The graph has retry/idempotency concepts for external side effects but no database concurrency concept where abort-and-retry is itself part of the isolation contract.
items.interpretation: Database transaction retry is modeled separately from idempotent receiver or workflow retry so external side-effect safety is not inferred from database retry semantics.

records.summary: DuckDB adds a deployment/composition model—analytical SQL inside the host process with direct file access—while independently reinforcing MVCC as a concurrency primitive already established by the PostgreSQL case. Retrieved workflow/execution concepts remain explicitly rejected as unrelated.

items.label: In-process analytical database
items.source_basis: DuckDB's core architecture runs the analytical DBMS inside the host application process rather than requiring a separate database server for normal embedded use.
items.prior_basis: Existing graph knowledge covered workflow execution and database concurrency but not the deployment boundary where analytical SQL itself becomes an application-local capability.
items.interpretation: In-process analytics becomes a reusable architecture choice about where the query engine lives, not a DuckDB feature checklist.

items.label: Embedded query engine
items.source_basis: Native client APIs let host code invoke DuckDB directly and work close to application data without provisioning a separate database service for the embedded use case.
items.prior_basis: No prior concept represented analytical query execution as a host-process library/runtime capability.
items.interpretation: The engine can be designed as a local component first, with a service boundary added only when sharing, lifecycle or governance requirements justify it.

items.label: Direct file querying
items.source_basis: DuckDB demonstrates SQL directly over CSV and Parquet, with official Parquet scans supporting projection and filter pushdown.
items.prior_basis: Earlier database concepts modeled native storage, WAL and MVCC rather than files as a directly queryable analytical layer.
items.interpretation: Some analytical pipelines can omit a mandatory load-to-database staging step and query files where they already live.

items.label: Multiversion Concurrency Control (MVCC)
items.source_basis: DuckDB documents MVCC together with optimistic concurrency control for multiple writer threads inside its single read-write process.
items.prior_basis: The PostgreSQL case already established MVCC as a database concurrency model that separates visible versions from concurrent physical updates.
items.interpretation: DuckDB reinforces MVCC as a reusable concurrency primitive while showing that MVCC does not define the surrounding process-ownership or client/server architecture by itself.

records.summary: LangGraph adds an explicit stateful-agent-orchestration layer and refines existing controlled/durable-execution knowledge without collapsing into ReAct or Temporal. The useful change is responsibility separation: reasoning strategy, graph orchestration state and broader execution governance are different layers.

items.label: Stateful agent orchestration
items.source_basis: LangGraph is positioned as a low-level orchestration framework/runtime for long-running stateful agents, with explicit graph state and control flow.
items.prior_basis: The graph already contains agent reasoning, durable workflow execution and controlled execution, but not a dedicated application-level graph orchestration concept that mixes deterministic and LLM-driven steps.
items.interpretation: Agent reasoning can now be placed inside an explicit orchestration layer rather than conflated with the whole application runtime.

items.label: Graph state checkpoint
items.source_basis: LangGraph checkpointers persist thread-scoped graph state for continuity, interruption, time travel and fault recovery.
items.prior_basis: Existing execution-history and Temporal concepts represent other durability models, but not LangGraph's thread-scoped graph-state checkpoint abstraction.
items.interpretation: This creates a concrete persistence boundary for agent orchestration while preserving the distinction from general workflow event histories.

items.label: Cross-thread store
items.source_basis: LangGraph Stores hold application-defined data across graph threads, separate from one thread's checkpointed execution state.
items.prior_basis: The current graph does not explicitly distinguish execution-state persistence from cross-thread agent/application memory.
items.interpretation: Persistence should be split by scope: thread execution continuity versus durable information reused across threads.

items.label: Controlled execution
items.source_basis: LangGraph provides explicit state, deterministic/agentic control flow, persistence and human-intervention points.
items.prior_basis: Controlled execution already includes a broader requirement for consequential work to be governable, reconstructable and testable.
items.interpretation: LangGraph refines the orchestration/persistence slice of controlled execution but does not supply authorization policy or protected-data governance by itself.

items.label: Durable execution
items.source_basis: Checkpointers let LangGraph threads preserve state through interruptions/failures and resume later.
items.prior_basis: Durable execution is already represented through the broader architecture case and the Temporal workflow model.
items.interpretation: LangGraph adds a domain-specific agent-graph durability mechanism; it reinforces the goal while refining how state is represented in this runtime.

records.summary: Docker build caching adds a new build-systems domain to the graph. Prior retrieval correctly found no close concepts, so the case introduces cache dependency boundaries and invalidation cascades without merging them into workflow checkpoints, database checkpoints or agent memory.

items.label: Build-cache dependency boundary
items.source_basis: Docker reuses a layer only while its instruction and dependent files remain unchanged, making cache reuse depend on explicit inputs.
items.prior_basis: The graph has persistence and checkpoint concepts in other domains, but no concept for build-result reuse controlled by instruction/input stability.
items.interpretation: Layer ordering and build-context design are best understood as editing the dependency boundary around expensive work.

items.label: Cache invalidation cascade
items.source_basis: Docker documentation states that a changed step causes following steps to rebuild, so frequent changes early in a Dockerfile amplify downstream work.
items.prior_basis: No current concept captures downstream build-cost fan-out caused by an upstream cache miss.
items.interpretation: The optimization target is not maximal caching in general; it is minimizing unnecessary invalidation fan-out from volatile inputs.

items.label: Persistent build cache
items.source_basis: Cache mounts retain package caches across layer rebuilds, and external caches allow cache reuse across different builders/environments.
items.prior_basis: Existing durable-state concepts have different semantics and should not be reused merely because data persists across runs.
items.interpretation: Persistent build cache is a cost-reduction mechanism for recomputation/downloads, not authoritative workflow or business state.

records.summary: NIST AI RMF opens a new AI-governance branch: a cross-cutting governance function plus context mapping, risk measurement and explicit risk response. No prior graph concept is close enough to reuse without collapsing implementation controls into the framework itself.

items.label: AI RMF Core
items.source_basis: AI RMF 1.0 organizes practical AI risk management around GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE and MANAGE outcomes and explicitly says the actions are not a checklist or mandatory ordered steps.
items.prior_basis: The project has architecture, policy, observability and decision concepts but no use-case-agnostic AI risk-management operating framework.
items.interpretation: The Core becomes a reusable layer for structuring AI risk decisions without pretending that one control implementation equals the framework.

items.label: Cross-cutting AI governance
items.source_basis: GOVERN is designed to inform and be infused throughout MAP, MEASURE and MANAGE rather than ending after an initial setup phase.
items.prior_basis: Existing governance-related concepts describe specific execution or policy mechanisms, not organizational accountability and risk culture across an AI lifecycle.
items.interpretation: Governance is modeled as persistent organizational capability and decision ownership rather than a one-time compliance gate.

items.label: AI risk context mapping
items.source_basis: MAP recognizes context, purpose, affected actors and context-related risks before those risks are measured or managed.
items.prior_basis: No prior concept explicitly models AI risk as dependent on deployment context and affected actors.
items.interpretation: Context becomes a prerequisite for selecting evidence and controls instead of treating generic model metrics as universally meaningful.

items.label: AI risk measurement and monitoring
items.source_basis: MEASURE applies quantitative, qualitative or mixed methods to assess, benchmark and monitor mapped AI risks and trustworthiness-related impacts.
items.prior_basis: Existing project evaluation/observability concepts do not provide a general AI risk-assessment function tied to context and risk-management decisions.
items.interpretation: Measurement is treated as evidence for risk decisions, not as telemetry volume or model benchmarking for its own sake.

items.label: AI risk prioritization and response
items.source_basis: MANAGE prioritizes assessed risks, develops responses and includes explicit determinations about whether development or deployment should proceed.
items.prior_basis: No prior concept provides a general lifecycle risk-response function that converts assessment results into proceed/mitigate/monitor/stop decisions.
items.interpretation: The framework's value culminates in visible risk decisions and treatment, not merely in documenting risks or measurements.

records.summary: The Transformer source opens a new neural sequence-architecture branch. All five scaffold-retrieved project concepts are rejected as cross-domain noise rather than forcing later learning/agent/governance ideas into the 2017 paper.

items.label: Transformer sequence-transduction architecture
items.source_basis: The paper proposes an encoder-decoder architecture based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolution for sequence transduction.
items.prior_basis: The graph had agent/runtime, learning and data-system concepts but no neural sequence-transduction architecture.
items.interpretation: The original Transformer is modeled as its 2017 encoder-decoder architecture rather than being retroactively collapsed into the broader modern LLM category.

items.label: Self-attention
items.source_basis: Encoder self-attention lets each encoder position attend to all positions in the previous layer; decoder self-attention does the same under a future-position mask.
items.prior_basis: No prior project concept represents neural attention among sequence positions.
items.interpretation: Self-attention becomes a neural sequence mechanism, separate from ReAct observation feedback or human attention/retrieval concepts.

items.label: Sequence-computation parallelism
items.source_basis: Table 1 compares full self-attention at O(1) sequential operations per layer with recurrent layers at O(n), one of the paper's main motivations for attention-only sequence layers.
items.prior_basis: No prior concept models neural sequence parallelism created by removing recurrent layer dependencies.
items.interpretation: Parallelism is retained as a specific computational-graph advantage, not as a claim that autoregressive output generation becomes fully parallel.

items.label: Attention dependency path
items.source_basis: Table 1 gives full self-attention O(1) maximum path length between positions versus O(n) for recurrent layers.
items.prior_basis: The graph has causal/process relations but no neural-network path-length model for sequence dependencies.
items.interpretation: Short dependency paths are kept as a separate reason self-attention can help long-range dependency learning rather than merged with generic performance claims.

items.label: Positional encoding
items.source_basis: Because the model contains no recurrence and no convolution, the paper adds positional encodings to input embeddings so sequence order is represented.
items.prior_basis: No prior project concept describes explicit positional information in an attention-only neural sequence model.
items.interpretation: Removing recurrence creates a new responsibility: order is no longer supplied by the recurrence structure and must be injected explicitly.
